nodes: Stored in a cornerstone; water damage followed

records.caption: The surviving manuscript brings us close to the work of the scribes, but it also carries the marks of loss. The Joseph Smith Papers documents its damage and preservation. This timeline helps us remember why an intact passage and a missing passage cannot answer the same questions.

records.title: Compare the English texts
nodes: Read the passage in its setting
What agrees, what differs, and how should it be explained?
records.footer: A textual relationship does not, by itself, explain how translation occurred.
records.caption: Royal Skousen’s study pays close attention to biblical quotations in the Book of Mormon. Reading the passages beside one another allows both agreements and differences to come into view. This guide separates an observable relationship in the English wording from a proposed explanation of how that wording came to be.
records.alt: Compare the English texts. King James Bible: Read the passage in its setting. Book of Mormon: Compare the corresponding passage. The scholarly question: What agrees, what differs, and how should it be explained?. A textual relationship does not, by itself, explain how translation occurred.

records.title: Two published testimonies
nodes: An angel showed the plates; they heard God’s voice
Joseph showed the plates; they saw and handled them
Different stated experiences belong in the comparison
records.footer: These are summaries of the statements, not reconstructed signatures.
records.caption: The two published statements invite careful listening. The Three describe an angel and a divine voice. The Eight describe seeing and handling plates shown by Joseph Smith. Reading both in their own words preserves the character of each testimony and gives us a sounder starting point for the later accounts.

records.title: A pattern you can follow
records.footer: Follow the reversed sequence, then return to Alma’s teaching about restoration.
records.caption: Alma’s counsel moves through four qualities and then returns through them in reverse order. The matching colors trace the relationship while preserving the different word forms in the verses. This small example invites a close reading of the passage; it does not settle a claim about the book’s origin.

nodes: The writers included in the study
The author may be outside that group
records.footer: Changing the candidate set can change the conclusion.
records.caption: A comparison can only answer the question its design allows. Schaalje and his colleagues examined an approach that does not assume the author is among the named candidates. This diagram illustrates that distinction. It contains no calculated scores and should not be read as the result of an authorship test.

records.title: An inscription and a proposal
nodes: NHM appears in ancient South Arabian inscriptions
Ishmael is buried at a place called Nahom
Scholars compare the consonants and regional setting
records.footer: The inscription is an artifact; the identification remains an argument.
records.caption: An ancient inscription and a scriptural place-name can be brought into conversation without making them identical. Warren Aston argues for a connection between NHM and Nahom. This guide keeps the inscription, Nephi’s account, and the proposed identification distinct. The letters shown are a modern transliteration, not a copied ancient inscription.

records.title: What can a name tell us?
nodes: Alma and a Hebrew root for youth or lad
Examine the form and proposed derivation
A possible derivation does not identify a person
records.footer: Read the worked example before drawing a larger conclusion.
records.caption: Paul Hoskisson offers a Hebrew derivation for the name Alma. His proposal gives readers a specific argument to examine instead of a list of names to accept at a glance. Notice the difference between a possible linguistic connection and evidence identifying a particular person or establishing the history of a whole record.

records.title: Keep the dates in view
nodes: Horses in the northern Rockies and central plains
European accounts came after this integration
This study does not establish Book of Mormon-era horses
records.footer: Earlier than some written accounts does not mean every earlier period.
records.caption: The 2023 study brings archaeological and other evidence into a history long told through later European accounts. Its findings illuminate Indigenous relationships with horses in the early seventeenth century. Keeping that period visible honors the study’s contribution while leaving the much earlier Book of Mormon question open.

records.title: Three questions for a metal
nodes: Copper and copper alloys at Mayapan
records.footer: These findings do not establish earlier steel production.
records.caption: The Mayapan study describes skilled metalworking in a particular place and period. Copper alloys, casting, and remelting deserve attention on their own terms. Keeping material, technique, and date together helps us appreciate that achievement without treating it as evidence for a different metal in a much earlier setting.

records.title: Ancestry and identification
nodes: Genetic research traces relationships among populations
Lehi’s own DNA profile is unknown
Ancestry evidence does not identify Lehi’s descendants
records.footer: The Church essay cautions against claiming DNA settles the book’s authenticity.
records.caption: Population history and the identification of a named family are different questions. The Church’s essay explains why the absence of a known genetic profile for Lehi matters. Read its discussion alongside the research cited above, keeping the evidence for ancient populations distinct from a claim to have identified Book of Mormon descendants.
